AbstractText.Label: CONTEXT
AbstractText.content: Epidemiologic studies have indicated that early life nutrition influences later risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and metabolic syndrome. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is also considered a metabolic disease.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: The aim was to explore the association between adult NAFLD and fetal or childhood exposure to Great Chinese Famine between 1959 and 1962 during fetal and childhood period.

AbstractText.Label: DESIGN AND SETTING
AbstractText.content: In total, 5306 subjects from the Survey on Prevalence in East China for Metabolic Diseases and Risk Factors study were divided into a fetal-exposed (1959-1962), childhood-exposed (1949-1958), adolescence/young adult-exposed (1921-1948), and nonexposed (1963-1974, reference) group.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE
AbstractText.content: The degrees of steatosis of NAFLD were determined by ultrasonography.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: The prevalences of NAFLD in the nonexposed (1963-1974), fetal-exposed, and childhood-exposed participants were 55.9%, 55.8%, and 55.4% in men and 33.0%, 46.3%, and 51.7% in women, respectively. Compared with those nonexposed, fetal- and childhood-exposed women but not men had a significantly higher prevalence of moderate-severe steatosis (P < .05). A significant association existed in women between increased alanine aminotransferase and both fetal and childhood exposure to famine, after adjusting for age, rural/urban residence, economic status, body mass index, diabetes, dyslipidemia, and hypertension (both P < .05). Famine exposure during the fetal period (odds ratio 1.77, 95% confidence interval 1.22, 2.57) and childhood (odds ratio 1.82, 95% confidence interval 1.35, 2.46) was associated with an increased prevalence of moderate-severe NAFLD in women in the above fully adjusted model.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSIONS
AbstractText.content: Exposure to the Great Famine in early life had sex-specific association with moderate-severe NAFLD. This indicates that malnutrition in early life may influence the development of adult NAFLD; thus pregnant women and their infants and children may require the highest priority in obtaining nutritional relief.
